# Model Architecture Modifications

Also called: NeRF Architecture Variants, Neural Radiance Field Structural Changes

## Overview
Model Architecture Modifications encompass structural changes to the standard Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) framework, which typically consists of two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) mapping spatial coordinates and viewing directions to volume density and color [S6]. These modifications address limitations in standard NeRF regarding geometric accuracy, rendering speed, dynamic scene handling, and semantic understanding. Unlike [NeRF Hyperparameters](3065-nerf-hyperparameters.md), which tune training configurations, this family alters the network topology, input/output signatures, or the underlying spatial representation (e.g., replacing MLPs with voxel grids or SDFs) to enable new capabilities such as real-time rendering, depth-of-field simulation, or sparse-view generalization.

## Shared principles
The standard NeRF architecture [S6] serves as the baseline for these modifications. It consists of a coarse network and a fine network. The coarse network takes positional encoded position $\gamma(\mathbf{x})$ and outputs a latent feature vector $\mathbf{h}$ and volume density $\sigma$. The fine network takes $\mathbf{h}$, positional encoded position $\gamma(\mathbf{x})$, and positional encoded view direction $\gamma(\mathbf{d})$ to output color $\mathbf{c}$.

$$
\gamma(\mathbf{x}, d_1, d_2) = [\mathbf{x}, \sin(2^{d_1}\pi\mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{d_1}\pi\mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{d_2-1}\pi\mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{d_2-1}\pi\mathbf{x})]
$$

Modifications generally fall into three categories:
1.  **Input Expansion:** Adding new conditioning vectors (e.g., appearance embeddings $\mathbf{z}_i$, fluid volume $v$, or previous stage RGB) to the input concatenation.
2.  **Output Expansion:** Adding auxiliary heads to predict values other than $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{c}$, such as semantic labels $y_{aux}$, object codes $o$, or area encoding probabilities $p$. These are rendered using the same transmittance weights $T_i$ and opacity $\alpha_i$ as color:
    $$
    \hat{Y}(r) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} T_i \alpha_i y_{aux}(x_i)
    $$
3.  **Representation Substitution:** Replacing the continuous MLP function with discrete structures (voxel grids, hash tables) or different implicit surfaces (SDFs).

## Subtopics

### [DoF-NeRF](9432-dof-nerf.md)
DoF-NeRF extends the standard NeRF architecture to simulate depth-of-field effects by introducing learnable aperture $K$ and focus distance $F$ parameters per view. It differs from siblings like [NeRF-VPT](11770-nerf-vpt.md) by explicitly modeling optical blur via the Circle of Confusion (CoC) diameter rather than refining image quality through iterative prompts. Choose this when synthesizing views with arbitrary focus configurations from shallow DoF inputs.

### [NeRF-VPT](11770-nerf-vpt.md)
NeRF-VPT is a cascading view prompt tuning paradigm that uses RGB information from preceding rendering iterations as visual prompts for subsequent stages. It differs from [MixRT](12401-mixrt.md) by relying on internal network outputs as priors rather than hybrid hardware pipelines. Choose this for sparse-view settings to iteratively refine image quality without external preprocessing.

### [MixRT](12401-mixrt.md)
MixRT is a hybrid representation combining a low-quality triangle mesh, a view-dependent displacement map, and a compressed NeRF model in an Instant-NGP hash table. It differs from [Activation Feature Density Approximation](12492-activation-feature-density-approximation.md) by offloading ray intersection to rasterizers and surface refinement to texture mapping units for real-time edge rendering. Choose this when rendering speed and storage efficiency on edge devices are critical.

### [Activation Feature Density Approximation](12492-activation-feature-density-approximation.md)
This method estimates volumetric density $\hat{d}$ directly from intermediate activation features $\mathbf{f}_\ell$ of a coordinate-based MLP, replacing expensive coarse network evaluations. It differs from [Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations](12495-signed-distance-function-sdf-representations.md) by retaining the standard density-based rendering formulation while optimizing the density prediction step itself. Choose this to accelerate training/inference by approximating density from hidden layer activations.

### [Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations](12495-signed-distance-function-sdf-representations.md)
SDF Representations replace volumetric density prediction with a continuous scalar field representing the distance to the nearest surface, defining geometry via a zero-level set. It differs from [Feature Fields](12995-feature-fields.md) by substituting the core implicit representation to enable sharper surface reconstruction. Choose this when geometric accuracy and explicit surface definition are prioritized over soft volumetric boundaries.

### [Volume-Augmented NeRF](12973-volume-augmented-nerf.md)
Volume-Augmented NeRF binds an explicit fluid volume value $v_i$ to each sample point, allowing density and color to change over time due to fluid flow. It differs from [Neural-PIL Decomposition Architecture](12975-neural-pil-decomposition-architecture.md) by integrating fluid simulation data directly into the radiance field rather than decomposing lighting. Choose this for dynamic scenes involving fluid dynamics.

### [Neural-PIL Decomposition Architecture](12975-neural-pil-decomposition-architecture.md)
This architecture separates scene geometry, material properties (BRDF), and illumination into distinct networks, using a learned pre-integrated lighting network. It differs from [Feature Fields](12995-feature-fields.md) by explicitly decoupling illumination for varying lighting conditions rather than adding semantic channels. Choose this when input images are captured under varying illumination and explicit reflectance decomposition is required.

### [Feature Fields](12995-feature-fields.md)
Feature Fields generalize NeRF by predicting arbitrary per-point feature signals $\mathbf{f}$ in addition to color and density, allowing 2D supervision to lift into a consistent 3D representation. It differs from [SAID-NeRF](13619-said-nerf.md) by integrating signals directly into the volume rendering pipeline rather than using semantic masks for robustness. Choose this for 3D-aware semantic understanding and object segmentation.

### [SAID-NeRF](13619-said-nerf.md)
SAID-NeRF exploits instance masks from Visual Foundation Models to enhance surface estimation of transparent objects by decomposing appearance into diffuse and specular components. It differs from [MINE](13661-mine.md) by using semantic segmentation for robustness rather than modeling the camera frustum with MPIs. Choose this for reconstructing transparent objects with sharp depth estimates.

### [MINE](13661-mine.md)
MINE models the frustum of the source camera using a continuous depth Multiplane Image (MPI) representation, conditioned on input images via a fully-convolutional decoder. It differs from [Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations](13738-voxel-and-sparse-grid-representations.md) by reconstructing the frustum per plane for efficient homography warping. Choose this for efficient novel view synthesis from single or few source views.

### [Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations](13738-voxel-and-sparse-grid-representations.md)
These representations replace the continuous MLP with discrete structures like 3D voxel grids, hash tables, or triplanes to store volume density and appearance features. It differs from [Aleth-NeRF](13764-aleth-nerf.md) by optimizing grid values for real-time rendering rather than modeling illumination adaptive volume rendering. Choose this for real-time differentiable volume rendering with reduced latency.

### [Aleth-NeRF](13764-aleth-nerf.md)
Aleth-NeRF trains on under- and over-exposed images to render normal-light novel views by introducing 'Concealing Fields' that model air particles attenuating emission. It differs from [Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA)](13784-unified-volumetric-avatar-uva.md) by handling low-light conditions via local/global concealing fields rather than anchoring latent codes to a deformable mesh. Choose this for synthesizing normal-light views from low-light or over-exposed inputs.

### [Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA)](13784-unified-volumetric-avatar-uva.md)
UVA represents dynamic human avatars by anchoring structured latent codes to a deformable mesh in canonical space, enabling local editing of geometry and texture. It differs from [Gear-NeRF](13848-gear-nerf.md) by supporting independent editing of geometry and texture rather than stratifying scenes into motion-based gears. Choose this for dynamic human avatars requiring local and independent editing.

### [Gear-NeRF](13848-gear-nerf.md)
Gear-NeRF leverages semantic information to stratify dynamic scenes into motion-based 'gears', allowing region-specific spatio-temporal sampling resolution. It differs from [Transformer and Vision Model Integration](13911-transformer-and-vision-model-integration.md) by using semantic segmentation for spatial stratification rather than global semantic understanding. Choose this for efficient free-viewpoint rendering of dynamic scenes with varying motion scales.

### [Transformer and Vision Model Integration](13911-transformer-and-vision-model-integration.md)
This family integrates Vision Transformers (ViT) into NeRFs to leverage global semantic understanding and long-range dependencies. It differs from [Human and Specific Subject Modeling](13997-human-and-specific-subject-modeling.md) by generalizing across scenes or modeling self-occlusion via attention rather than focusing on specific subject types. Choose this when global scene modeling or single-image input handling is required.

### [Human and Specific Subject Modeling](13997-human-and-specific-subject-modeling.md)
This family focuses on architectures tailored for specific subjects, such as humans, often leveraging prior knowledge or specialized deformation fields. It differs from [OPONeRF](14014-oponerf.md) by targeting specific subject categories rather than dynamically conditioning network weights per point. Choose this for high-fidelity reconstruction of specific subject types like humans.

### [OPONeRF](14014-oponerf.md)
OPONeRF personalizes plenoptic mapping function parameters for each sampled 3D point by dynamically conditioning network weights on the point's representation and scene representation. It differs from [Mixer-NeRF](14073-mixer-nerf.md) by subdividing the scene and discriminatively responding to local variations rather than mixing spatial and channel features. Choose this for handling test-time scene changes and robustness against perturbations.

### [Mixer-NeRF](14073-mixer-nerf.md)
Mixer-NeRF addresses blurry details by introducing a hybrid spatial feature learning module (MLCA) and a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) network module. It differs from [SCALAR-NeRF](14267-scalar-nerf.md) by explicitly mixing spatial and channel features via fully connected layers rather than decomposing scenes into spatial blocks. Choose this for improving local information and detail in 3D reconstruction.

### [SCALAR-NeRF](14267-scalar-nerf.md)
SCALAR-NeRF is a coarse-to-fine framework for large-scale scenes that decomposes expansive scenes into spatial blocks, sharing a global decoder. It differs from [Sparse View and Few-Shot Optimization](14428-sparse-view-and-few-shot-optimization.md) by using block-based fusion with a global reference model rather than in-situ regularization for sparse views. Choose this for scalable large-scale neural scene reconstruction on a single GPU.

### [Sparse View and Few-Shot Optimization](14428-sparse-view-and-few-shot-optimization.md)
This family addresses overfitting and artifact generation in NeRFs trained with drastically reduced viewpoints ($|S| < 20$). It differs from [Mixture-of-Experts and Modular Architectures](14429-mixture-of-experts-and-modular-architectures.md) by mitigating ambiguity through regularization and deformable sampling rather than partitioning the input domain among experts. Choose this when training with sparse input views.

### [Mixture-of-Experts and Modular Architectures](14429-mixture-of-experts-and-modular-architectures.md)
This family replaces the single continuous function of NeRF with multiple specialized networks (experts) or parallel processing streams. It differs from [Uncertainty and Reliability](14487-uncertainty-and-reliability.md) by explicitly partitioning the input domain among distinct neural modules rather than modeling error distributions. Choose this to improve compression, training speed, or representation capacity for complex features.

### [Uncertainty and Reliability](14487-uncertainty-and-reliability.md)
These methods extend NeRF architectures to quantify prediction confidence, modeling the scene as a probabilistic entity. It differs from [Object Decomposition and Composition](14518-object-decomposition-and-composition.md) by providing pixel-level reliability metrics rather than decomposing the scene into object instances. Choose this for robust filtering and conformal prediction in sparse or unstructured data.

### [Object Decomposition and Composition](14518-object-decomposition-and-composition.md)
This family explicitly separates a scene into distinct semantic or geometric object instances for instance-level editing. It differs from [Lighting and Appearance Models](14522-lighting-and-appearance-models.md) by focusing on structural decomposition for editing rather than decoupling illumination. Choose this for amodal segmentation and object manipulation.

### [Lighting and Appearance Models](14522-lighting-and-appearance-models.md)
These models modify the color prediction head to decouple scene geometry from illumination variations and transient artifacts. It differs from [Optimization and Training Procedures](14565-optimization-and-training-procedures.md) by learning implicit appearance embeddings or pre-integrated lighting queries rather than modifying the optimization scope. Choose this for real-world image collections with lighting changes.

### [Optimization and Training Procedures](14565-optimization-and-training-procedures.md)
This family covers algorithmic procedures for optimizing NeRFs, including structural modifications to the optimization scope. It differs from [Image Enhancement and Restoration Methods](14566-image-enhancement-and-restoration-methods.md) by focusing on efficient loss minimization and gradient management rather than integrating restoration mechanisms. Choose this for managing computational constraints during training.

### [Image Enhancement and Restoration Methods](14566-image-enhancement-and-restoration-methods.md)
These methods address input imagery degradation (blur, occlusions) by integrating restoration mechanisms into the NeRF loop. It differs from [Modular, Hierarchical, and Latent Architectures](14567-modular-hierarchical-and-latent-architectures.md) by focusing on specific degradation types like optical blur rather than handling non-rigid deformation. Choose this for rendering clean novel views from degraded inputs.

### [Modular, Hierarchical, and Latent Architectures](14567-modular-hierarchical-and-latent-architectures.md)
This family extends NeRFs to handle non-rigid deformation with topological changes and hierarchical scene structures. It differs from [NeRF-W](14630-nerf-w.md) by lifting canonical space into higher dimensions or using discrete latent codes rather than disentangling static geometry from transient elements. Choose this for scenes with topological variations or hierarchical levels.

### [NeRF-W](14630-nerf-w.md)
NeRF-W handles unconstrained, "in-the-wild" photo collections by disentangling shared static geometry from image-dependent transient elements and photometric variations. It differs from [Generalizable Implicit Reconstruction with SRDF](14760-generalizable-implicit-reconstruction-with-srdf.md) by combining appearance and uncertainty modeling rather than using Signed Ray Distance Functions. Choose this for reconstructing high-frequency details in unconstrained photo collections.

### [Generalizable Implicit Reconstruction with SRDF](14760-generalizable-implicit-reconstruction-with-srdf.md)
VolRecon uses a Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF) and a ray transformer to aggregate features from multi-view images. It differs from [MuRF (Multi-Baseline Radiance Fields)](15007-murf-multi-baseline-radiance-fields.md) by capturing local geometric cues and global context via SRDF rather than constructing a target view frustum volume. Choose this for fine-detail reconstruction with low noise from sparse views.

### [MuRF (Multi-Baseline Radiance Fields)](15007-murf-multi-baseline-radiance-fields.md)
MuRF is a feed-forward method for sparse view synthesis that constructs a target view frustum volume aligned with the target camera. It differs from [Gaussian and Primitive-Based Representations](15011-gaussian-and-primitive-based-representations.md) by using a 3D context-aware convolutional decoder rather than analytic primitives. Choose this for novel view synthesis under varying camera baselines.

### [Gaussian and Primitive-Based Representations](15011-gaussian-and-primitive-based-representations.md)
This family replaces the continuous MLP with discrete geometric primitives or explicit Gaussian distributions. It differs from [Decentralized Federated NeRF](15032-decentralized-federated-nerf.md) by using alpha-blended primitives rather than distributing training computation. Choose this for improved rendering efficiency and geometric fidelity.

### [Decentralized Federated NeRF](15032-decentralized-federated-nerf.md)
DecentNeRF learns global 3D scene representations from crowd-sourced images by distributing training computation and aggregating global models. It differs from [Tile and Slide Framework](15219-tile-and-slide-framework.md) by decomposing the scene into global and personal radiance fields per user rather than dividing the region into non-overlapping tiles. Choose this for privacy-preserving global scene reconstruction from crowdsourced data.

### [Tile and Slide Framework](15219-tile-and-slide-framework.md)
This out-of-core framework scales NeRFs to large scenes by dividing the region into non-overlapping 3D tiles, each trained with its own NeRF. It differs from [Neural Proxy](15220-neural-proxy.md) by operating on spatial tiles rather than representing targets as animatable proxies. Choose this for large-scale scene reconstruction (e.g., 10km x 10km) on a single GPU.

### [Neural Proxy](15220-neural-proxy.md)
A neural rendering model that represents photo-realistic targets as animatable proxies to enable rendering of unseen animations. It differs from [DoF-NeRF](9432-dof-nerf.md) by combining neural volume rendering and neural texture for animation rather than simulating depth-of-field. Choose this for rendering unseen animations without temporal learning.

#### NeRF-VAE
- **Definition:** A generative NeRF model that generalizes to out-of-distribution scenes and removes the need to train on each scene from scratch [S1].
- **Step:** The NeRF renderer is conditioned on a latent code trained using Iterative Amortized Inference and a ResNet encoder. An attention-based scene function is introduced instead of the typical MLP [S1].
- **Comparison:** Outperforms baseline NeRF with a low number of scene views (5-20), but is outperformed by baseline NeRF when a large number of views are available (100+) due to lower scene expressivity [S1].

#### PIE-NeRF
- **Definition:** A pipeline integrating physics-based elastodynamic simulation with a neural radiance field representation, using a meshless discretisation based on quadratic generalized moving least squares on top of the density field of a NeRF [S1].
- **Step:** Enables large deformations and nonlinear hyperelastic material simulation directly on the implicit representation and supports interactive manipulation of real-world captured scenes with complex geometries [S1].

#### DäRF Implementation Details
- **Parameter:** NeRF Backbone: K-planes [36]. MDE Model: DPT-hybrid [38]. Optimizer: Adam [21]. NeRF Learning Rate: 1e-2. MDE Learning Rate: 1e-5. LR Schedule: Cosine warmup [S2, unofficial].

#### NeRF Model Architecture
- **Definition:** The neural network architecture for NeRF, consisting of dense layers with ReLU activations, potentially using view directions as input [S3, unofficial].
- **Parameter:** `D`: The depth of the network (number of hidden layers). Default is 8. `input_ch_views`: The number of input channels for view directions. Default is 3. `output_ch`: The number of output channels. Default is 4 (RGB + density). `use_viewdirs`: Boolean flag to determine if view directions are used as input to the network [S3, unofficial].

#### S3-NeRF
- **Definition:** A method using shadow and shading cues to infer scene geometry and enable single-image NeRF training [S1].
- **Step:** Employ a UNISURF-based occupancy field 3D representation instead of density. Use a modified physics-based rendering equation. Use occupancy-based shadow calculation [S1].

#### KiloNeRF-style Grid Distillation
- **Definition:** Distills a large teacher NeRF into a spatially partitioned grid of tiny MLPs to enable fast, adaptive evaluation by mapping 3D positions to local student networks [S4, unofficial].
- **Step:** Initialize a dictionary mapping 3D grid cell indices (i,j,k) to TinyMLP instances. For each training iteration, sample a random ray and generate num_samples stratified samples along it. Compute the grid cell index for each sample by normalizing its position within the bounding box and scaling by grid resolution. Accumulate L2 loss between student and teacher outputs across all samples. Update all grid MLPs using the accumulated loss and the configured learning rate [S4, unofficial].
- **Parameter:** grid_resolution: 3D tuple defining the number of cells per axis, e.g., (16,16,16). num_distill_iterations: Number of distillation optimization steps, e.g., 1000. num_samples: Number of stratified samples per ray, e.g., 384. learning_rate: Optimization step size for grid MLP updates, e.g., 1e-3. bmin, bmax: Axis-aligned bounding box defining the scene bounds, e.g., [0,0,0] and [1,1,1] [S4, unofficial].

#### NeRF with Time Parameter
- **Step:** Add a time parameter to the model inputs to adapt NeRF for dynamic scenes. Positionally encode the time parameter and concatenate it with the positional encoding of spatial coordinates $\gamma_x(\mathbf{x})$ [S5].
- **Parameter:** Train using the configuration reported for NeRF's real forward-facing experiments [S5].
- **Comparison:** Adding a time parameter improves quality over vanilla NeRF but still lacks detail, suffers from blurry predictions, and fails to reason about scene dynamics [S5].

#### StylizedNeRF
- **Step:** Utilizes a mutual learning strategy to optimize both the stylized NeRF and the 2D stylization network. Handles ambiguities of the 2D stylized results via learnable latent codes, ensuring consistency in geometry [S6].

#### NeRF-Editing
- **Definition:** The first mesh-based shape deformation method, leveraging explicit representations for scene geometry edits and implicit representations for realistic rendering effects [S6].
- **Step:** 1. Extract explicit triangular mesh from NeRF. 2. Enable intuitive user-driven deformations through classic ARAP deformation method. 3. Generate tetrahedral mesh around triangular mesh to propagate deformations spatially. 4. Employ tetrahedral vertex interpolation to transform discrete deformations into continuous field. 5. Ensure rays passing through mesh bend according to user adjustments [S6].

#### NeuralEditor
- **Definition:** A method employing a point cloud-guided NeRF model for shape manipulation, leveraging K-D trees and deterministic integration strategy for accurate point cloud-based rendering, with Phong reflection modeling to enhance color fidelity and geometric detail [S6].
- **Step:** 1. Employ point cloud-guided NeRF model. 2. Leverage K-D trees. 3. Use deterministic integration strategy. 4. Achieve accurate point cloud-based rendering. 5. Apply Phong reflection modeling [S6].

#### Shared G-MLP
- **Definition:** A shared geometry MLP that enables the constraint of multi-view consistency to be propagated from the NeRF branch to the detection branch [S7].
- **Number:** Without the shared G-MLP, performance drops from 50.1 to 48.1 mAP@.25, as the influence of multi-view consistency is only propagated into the image backbone [S7].

#### Mip-NeRF
- **Definition:** A method that approximates cone tracing instead of using the ray tracing of standard NeRF volume rendering to achieve inherent multi-scale representation and automatic anti-aliasing, outperforming baseline NeRF especially at lower resolutions [S1].
- **Step:** To generate an individual pixel, a cone is cast from the camera center along the viewing direction through the center of the pixel. The cone is approximated by a multivariate Gaussian whose mean vector and covariance matrix are derived to match the appropriate geometry [S1].
- **Formula:** The Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) is calculated as: $\gamma(\mu, \Sigma) = E_{x \sim N(\mu, \Sigma)}[\gamma(x)] = \begin{bmatrix} \sin(\mu_\gamma) \odot \exp(-(1/2)\text{diag}(\Sigma_\gamma)) \\ \cos(\mu_\gamma) \odot \exp(-(1/2)\text{diag}(\Sigma_\gamma)) \end{bmatrix}$, where $\mu_\gamma, \Sigma_\gamma$ are the means and variances of the multivariate Gaussian lifted onto the positional encoding basis with N levels [S1].
- **Comparison:** Unlike standard NeRF which uses ray tracing, Mip-NeRF uses cone tracing via IPE, resulting in automatic anti-aliasing and better performance at lower resolutions [S1].

## Background
The standard NeRF architecture was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020 [S1][S3, unofficial]. Subsequent modifications have aimed to address its limitations in speed, geometric accuracy, and applicability to dynamic or sparse-view scenarios. Key developments include Mip-NeRF (2021) for anti-aliasing [S1], Instant-NGP for hash-based acceleration [S1], and various extensions for dynamic scenes, lighting, and semantics. The field has evolved from pure MLP-based representations to hybrid, voxel-based, and primitive-based approaches to enable real-time rendering and broader applicability [S1].
